claim: Loop extrusion by structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes has been proposed as a mechanism to organize chromatin in interphase and metaphase.
source: Loop extrusion by structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes has been proposed as a mechanism to organize chromatin in interphase and metaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature proposing the loop extrusion hypothesis.

claim: Loops form in both metaphase and interphase, but with distinct dynamic properties.
source: We show that loops form in both metaphase and interphase, but with distinct dynamic properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript showing loop formation in both cell cycle phases.

claim: Condensin extrudes DNA loops non-symmetrically in metaphase.
source: Condensin extrudes DNA loops non-symmetrically in metaphase, whereas cohesin extrudes loops symmetrically in interphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the symmetry properties of loop extrusion in metaphase.

claim: Cohesin extrudes loops symmetrically in interphase.
source: Condensin extrudes DNA loops non-symmetrically in metaphase, whereas cohesin extrudes loops symmetrically in interphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the symmetry properties of loop extrusion in interphase.

claim: Loop extrusion is a general mechanism underlying DNA organization, with dynamic and structural properties that are biochemically regulated during the cell cycle.
source: Our data show that loop extrusion is a general mechanism underlying DNA organization, with dynamic and structural properties that are biochemically regulated during the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing differential regulation of loop extrusion in different cell cycle phases.

claim: Chromatin undergoes a dramatic reorganization during the cell cycle.
source: Chromatin undergoes a dramatic reorganization during the cell cycle (Hirano and Mitchison, 1991; Rowley and Corces, 2018; Nagano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In interphase, chromatin is organized into compartments and topological-associating domains (TADs) that are cell-type specific.
source: In interphase, chromatin is organized into compartments and topological-associating domains (TADs) that are cell-type specific (Bonev and Cavalli, 2016; Dekker and Mirny, 2016; Rao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TADs are composed of chromatin loops that have been hypothesized to regulate gene expression by spatially restricting contacts between genes and regulatory elements.
source: TADs are composed of chromatin loops that have been hypothesized to regulate gene expression by spatially restricting contacts between genes and regulatory elements (Smith et al., 2016; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2017; Schoenfelder and Fraser, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this hypothesis.

claim: In metaphase, chromosomes undergo large-scale compaction, leading to the loss of specific boundaries and the shutdown of transcription.
source: In metaphase, chromosomes undergo large-scale compaction, leading to the loss of specific boundaries and the shutdown of transcription, which is achieved by arranging chromatin into an array of condensed loops (Marsden and Laemmli, 1979; Earnshaw and Laemmli, 1983; Naumova et al., 2013; Goloborodko et al., 2016; Uhlmann, 2016; Kinoshita and Hirano, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Metaphase chromosome compaction is achieved by arranging chromatin into an array of condensed loops.
source: In metaphase, chromosomes undergo large-scale compaction, leading to the loss of specific boundaries and the shutdown of transcription, which is achieved by arranging chromatin into an array of condensed loops (Marsden and Laemmli, 1979; Earnshaw and Laemmli, 1983; Naumova et al., 2013; Goloborodko et al., 2016; Uhlmann, 2016; Kinoshita and Hirano, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SMCs are thought to organize DNA by actively extruding DNA loops.
source: SMCs are thought to organize DNA by actively extruding DNA loops (Rao et al., 2014; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Alipour and Marko, 2012; Sanborn et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast condensin extrudes DNA loops in a one-sided manner in vitro.
source: Recent experimental studies have shown that yeast condensin extrudes DNA loops in a one-sided manner in vitro (Ganji et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: One-sided loop extrusion by yeast condensin in vitro is inconsistent with the requirement for two-sided loop extrusion predicted by theory.
source: Although consistent with the loop-extrusion hypothesis, it is inconsistent with the requirement for two-sided loop extrusion predicted by theory (Banigan and Mirny, 2018; Banigan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: The properties of loop extrusion in cellular contexts may differ from those in vitro and may be regulated during the cell cycle.
source: One reason for this discrepancy could be that the properties of loop extrusion in cellular contexts differ from those in vitro and may be regulated during the cell cycle (Abramo et al., 2019; Losada et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents a hypothesis to explain observed discrepancies.

claim: Condensin complexes do not structure the genome during interphase.
source: Notably, condensin complexes do not structure the genome during interphase (Abdennur, 2018), which raises intriguing questions about the molecular players that regulate DNA architecture in interphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cohesin can extrude DNA loops symmetrically in vitro.
source: Recent in vitro work demonstrated that cohesin can extrude DNA loops symmetrically (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019), though this activity has not been directly visualized in cellular contexts (Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent in vitro studies.

claim: Cohesin's symmetric loop extrusion activity has not been directly visualized in cellular contexts.
source: Recent in vitro work demonstrated that cohesin can extrude DNA loops symmetrically (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019), though this activity has not been directly visualized in cellular contexts (Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating the absence of direct visualization in cellular contexts.

claim: Xenopus laevis egg extracts can be cycled between metaphase and interphase and recapitulate many sub-cellular biological processes.
source: These extracts can be cycled between metaphase and interphase and recapitulate many sub-cellular biological processes, such as the formation of mitotic chromatids and interphase nuclei (Hirano and Mitchison, 1991; Murray, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies establishing the properties of Xenopus egg extracts.

claim: Addition of either metaphase-arrested or interphase Xenopus egg extracts into the chamber triggered the formation of small DNA enrichments, consistent with nucleosomal deposition.
source: Addition of either metaphase-arrested or interphase Xenopus egg extracts into the chamber triggered the formation of small DNA enrichments, consistent with nucleosomal deposition (Yan et al., 2007; Gruszka et al., 2019), that rapidly reduced any slack in the DNA molecules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—videos 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations, citations, and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Depletion of ~90–95% of soluble H3-H4 heterodimers in the extract led to the formation of compacted DNA clusters that grew in size over time in both metaphase and interphase.
source: To increase the amount of available slack to allow for loop extrusion, we abolished nucleosomal assembly along the strand by depleting ~90–95% of soluble H3-H4 heterodimers in the extract (Zierhut et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). This led to the formation of compacted DNA clusters that grew in size over time in both metaphase and interphase (Figure 1B and Videos 1–2; Figure 1—videos 3–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, citation, and reference to figures and videos.

claim: Hydrodynamic stretching revealed DNA clusters with a characteristic loop topology in both inter- and metaphase extracts.
source: This procedure revealed DNA clusters with a characteristic loop topology in both inter- and metaphase extracts (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—video 1; Figure 1—videos 7–9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to figures and videos.

claim: In mock-depleted extracts, loops also formed but at a much lower frequency.
source: In mock-depleted extracts, loops also formed but at a much lower frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Figure 1—video 10) and seemed to compete with nucleosomes for available DNA slack.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: DNA loop extrusion can be reconstituted in Xenopus egg extracts in metaphase and interphase.
source: These results show that DNA loop extrusion can be reconstituted in Xenopus egg extracts in metaphase and interphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results described in the manuscript.

claim: DNA loops in metaphase-arrested, H3-H4-depleted extract are initially extruded at 2.36 ± 0.35 kb/s (mean ± SEM).
source: When applied to metaphase-arrested, H3-H4-depleted extract (n=7 extract days), this assay showed that DNA loops are initially extruded at 2.36 ± 0.35 kb/s (mean ± SEM) (Figure 2Bi, C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data and reference to figures.

claim: Loop growth rapidly slowed down as more DNA was pulled into the looped region.
source: However, loop growth rapidly slowed down as more DNA was pulled into the looped region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that extrusion rates depend on DNA tension.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Extrusion rates depend on DNA tension.
source: However, loop growth rapidly slowed down as more DNA was pulled into the looped region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that extrusion rates depend on DNA tension.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that loop growth slows as DNA tension increases.

claim: The relationship between extrusion rates and DNA tension is generally conserved for all looping events.
source: These results show that the relationship between extrusion rates and DNA tension is generally conserved for all looping events (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Loop extrusion in metaphase stopped when the relative extension of DNA outside of the loop reached on average ~65%, corresponding to a stall force of 0.16 pN ± 0.01 pN (mean ± SEM).
source: Finally, loop extrusion stopped when the relative extension of DNA outside of the loop reached on average ~65%, corresponding to a stall force of 0.16 pN ± 0.01 pN (mean ± SEM), (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data and reference to figures.

claim: In rare cases, individual looping events stalled at DNA extensions of up to ~85%, corresponding to forces up to ~1 pN.
source: In rare cases, we observed individual looping events stalling at DNA extensions of up to ~85%, corresponding to forces up to ~1 pN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The majority of metaphase looping events had a symmetry score close to 1, which corresponds to one-sided (non-symmetric) loop extrusion.
source: The majority of metaphase looping events had a symmetry score close to 1, which corresponds to one-sided (non-symmetric) loop extrusion (Figure 2Biii).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data and reference to figures.

claim: A small population of ~20% of all metaphase looping events were two-sided.
source: However, a small population of ~20% of all metaphase looping events were two-sided (as defined by a symmetry score of less than 0.5, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Loops that were displaced during loop formation in metaphase moved with equal probability towards the boundaries or the center of the strand.
source: Consistent with one-sided loop extrusion, loops that were displaced during loop formation, moved with equal probability towards the boundaries or the center of the strand.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of loop movement data.

claim: The equal probability of loop movement towards boundaries or center is suggestive of non-symmetric DNA extruding factors landing in a random orientation on the DNA molecule.
source: This behavior is suggestive of non-symmetric DNA extruding factors landing in a random orientation on the DNA molecule.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the observed loop movement patterns.

claim: DNA loop extrusion in metaphase is predominantly one-sided, with extrusion speeds and stall forces similar to those measured in vitro.
source: Taken together, our analysis demonstrates that DNA loop extrusion in metaphase is predominantly one-sided, with extrusion speeds and stall forces similar to those measured in vitro (Ganji et al., 2018; Strick et al., 2004; Kong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with cited in vitro studies.

claim: Loop extrusion in interphase displayed a mean extrusion rate of 1.94 ± 0.26 kb/s.
source: Loop extrusion in interphase displayed a similar distribution of extrusion rates, with a mean of 1.94 ± 0.26 kb/s, and average stall forces of 0.18 pN ±0.03 pN, with maximal forces of up to 0.82 pN (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data and reference to figures.

claim: Loop extrusion in interphase displayed average stall forces of 0.18 pN ±0.03 pN, with maximal forces of up to 0.82 pN.
source: Loop extrusion in interphase displayed a similar distribution of extrusion rates, with a mean of 1.94 ± 0.26 kb/s, and average stall forces of 0.18 pN ±0.03 pN, with maximal forces of up to 0.82 pN (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative experimental data and reference to figures.

claim: The distribution of symmetry scores of interphase looping events peaked towards zero, indicating that these loops are symmetrically extruded.
source: However, the distribution of symmetry scores of these looping events peaked towards zero, indicating that these loops are symmetrically extruded.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: A sub-population of ~20% of all interphase loops had the opposite symmetry (symmetry score larger than 0.5).
source: Similar to metaphase looping, we observed that a sub-population of ~20% of all loops had the opposite symmetry (symmetry score larger than 0.5, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Loops that started off-center on the strand in interphase displayed a strong bias to move towards the DNA boundary of the shorter DNA portion.
source: As predicted for symmetric extrusion, loops that started off-center on the strand displayed a strong bias to move towards the DNA boundary of the shorter DNA portion (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The mechanisms of DNA loop extrusion are different in interphase and metaphase.
source: Thus, we conclude that the mechanisms of DNA loop extrusion are different in interphase and metaphase.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing different symmetry properties.

claim: The cell cycle-dependent activities of condensin and cohesin could account for the transition between symmetric and non-symmetric loop extrusion.
source: The cell cycle-dependent activities of condensin and cohesin could account for the transition between symmetric and non-symmetric loop extrusion (Banigan et al., 2019; Abramo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: In metaphase, the occurrence of DNA loop extrusion was significantly reduced (p<0.01) upon depletion of condensin I and II but was unaffected by cohesin depletion.
source: We found that, in metaphase (n = 3 extract days), the occurrence of DNA loop extrusion was significantly reduced (p<0.01) upon depletion of condensin I and II but was unaffected by cohesin depletion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from depletion experiments and reference to figures.

claim: In interphase, there was a significant decrease (p<0.01) in loop extrusion following cohesin depletion but was unaffected by condensin depletion.
source: In contrast, there was a significant decrease (p<0.01) in loop extrusion following cohesin depletion in interphase (n = 3 extract days), but was unaffected by condensin depletion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from depletion experiments and reference to figures.

claim: Immunostainings showed colocalization of cohesin with the DNA loops observed in interphase.
source: We confirmed these depletions with immunostainings that showed colocalization of cohesin and condensin with the DNA loops observed in interphase and metaphase, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data and reference to figures.

claim: Immunostainings showed colocalization of condensin with the DNA loops observed in metaphase.
source: We confirmed these depletions with immunostainings that showed colocalization of cohesin and condensin with the DNA loops observed in interphase and metaphase, respectively (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data and reference to figures.

claim: Apyrase-mediated ATP depletion in interphase extract resulted in a near-complete elimination of DNA looping activity.
source: When applied to interphase extract, apyrase-mediated ATP depletion resulted in a near-complete elimination of DNA looping activity , suggesting that cohesin actively extrudes loops in an ATP-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATP depletion experiments.

claim: Cohesin actively extrudes loops in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: When applied to interphase extract, apyrase-mediated ATP depletion resulted in a near-complete elimination of DNA looping activity , suggesting that cohesin actively extrudes loops in an ATP-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ATP depletion eliminates looping activity in interphase.

claim: Cohesin actively extrudes DNA loops symmetrically during interphase, whereas condensin extrudes DNA loops non-symmetrically in metaphase.
source: Altogether, our results show that cohesin actively extrudes DNA loops symmetrically during interphase, whereas condensin extrudes DNA loops non-symmetrically in metaphase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data from loop dynamics and depletion experiments.

claim: The molecular mechanisms of DNA loop extrusion are differentially regulated during the cell cycle.
source: This demonstrates that the molecular mechanisms of DNA loop extrusion are differentially regulated during the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing different complexes are responsible for loop extrusion in different cell cycle phases.

claim: Loop extrusion is a general mechanism of DNA organization in a cellular context.
source: Our findings provide the first direct evidence that loop extrusion is a general mechanism of DNA organization in a cellular context, and, furthermore, that it is differentially regulated during the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental demonstration of loop extrusion in both cell cycle phases.

claim: Loop extrusion regulation is achieved by the distinct activities of cohesin and condensin during interphase and metaphase.
source: This regulation is achieved by the distinct activities of cohesin (Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Losada et al., 1998) and condensin (Kinoshita and Hirano, 2017; Hirano et al., 1997; Shintomi et al., 2017) during interphase and metaphase, and may control different levels of DNA organization during the cell cycle: from chromatin that is mostly decondensed and spatially organized into TAD structures during interphase to highly compacted chromosomes in metaphase (Abramo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to relevant studies.

claim: Symmetric loop extrusion by cohesin in interphase may ensure the formation of specific TAD boundaries by bringing together distal CTCF sites.
source: Symmetric loop extrusion by cohesin in interphase may ensure the formation of specific TAD boundaries by bringing together distal CTCF sites (Sanborn et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Reorganization of loosely packed interphase chromatin into condensed chromosomes leads to the loss of TAD boundaries and the shutdown of transcription.
source: In metaphase, reorganization of loosely packed interphase chromatin into condensed chromosomes leads to the loss of TAD boundaries and the shutdown of transcription (Nagano et al., 2017; Naumova et al., 2013), which may be achieved by condensin activity (Goloborodko et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The loss of TAD boundaries and shutdown of transcription in metaphase may be achieved by condensin activity.
source: In metaphase, reorganization of loosely packed interphase chromatin into condensed chromosomes leads to the loss of TAD boundaries and the shutdown of transcription (Nagano et al., 2017; Naumova et al., 2013), which may be achieved by condensin activity (Goloborodko et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to a relevant study.

claim: Condensin binds to chromatin in metaphase, but is largely undetected on chromatin in interphase.
source: Previous studies have shown that condensin binds to chromatin in metaphase, but is largely undetected on chromatin in interphase (Hirano and Mitchison, 1994); whereas cohesin is bound to chromatin in interphase, but not as strongly in metaphase (Losada et al., 1998; Sumara et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cohesin is bound to chromatin in interphase, but not as strongly in metaphase.
source: Previous studies have shown that condensin binds to chromatin in metaphase, but is largely undetected on chromatin in interphase (Hirano and Mitchison, 1994); whereas cohesin is bound to chromatin in interphase, but not as strongly in metaphase (Losada et al., 1998; Sumara et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CDK1-mediated phosphorylation of condensin HEAT subunits in metaphase may be the biochemical signal that triggers the association of condensin to chromatin.
source: The CDK1-mediated phosphorylation of condensin HEAT subunits in metaphase may be the biochemical signal that triggers the association of condensin to chromatin (Hirano et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to a relevant study.

claim: Most cohesin is released from chromatin by a mechanism that involves the phosphorylation of cohesin's SA subunit.
source: In contrast, most cohesin is released from chromatin by a mechanism that involves the phosphorylation of cohesin's SA subunit (Losada and Hirano, 2001; Hauf et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The different affinities of condensin and cohesin for chromatin during the cell cycle could be a natural explanation for the different DNA loop extrusion activities observed in the experiments.
source: Thus, the different affinities of condensin and cohesin for chromatin during the cell cycle could be a natural explanation for the different DNA loop extrusion activities that we see in our experiments.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis that connects known binding properties with observed experimental results.

claim: The demonstration of predominantly non-symmetric DNA loop extrusion during metaphase is consistent with recent in vitro data.
source: Our demonstration of predominantly non-symmetric DNA loop extrusion during metaphase is consistent with recent in vitro data, but it is at odds with the theoretical requirements to fully compact chromosomes in metaphase (Banigan and Mirny, 2018; Banigan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim compares the experimental findings with previous in vitro studies.

claim: Predominantly non-symmetric DNA loop extrusion during metaphase is at odds with the theoretical requirements to fully compact chromosomes in metaphase.
source: Our demonstration of predominantly non-symmetric DNA loop extrusion during metaphase is consistent with recent in vitro data, but it is at odds with the theoretical requirements to fully compact chromosomes in metaphase (Banigan and Mirny, 2018; Banigan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim compares the experimental findings with theoretical predictions.

claim: A small fraction of two-sided loop extruders can facilitate higher levels of chromosome compaction.
source: However, these studies suggest that a small fraction of two-sided loop extruders—including extrusion events that reel in DNA at different rates from left and right—can facilitate higher levels of chromosome compaction.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Loops with symmetry scores below 0.8 could be considered 'slow' two-sided extrusion events.
source: Our metaphase data suggest that loops with symmetry scores below 0.8 could be considered 'slow' two-sided extrusion events, as DNA is reeled into the loop from both sides, but at different rates.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Loops with symmetry scores below 0.8 account for about 50% of the total population of metaphase looping events.
source: These events account for about 50% of the total population of metaphase looping events, which, according to theoretical predictions, could be sufficient to achieve 100-fold linear chromosome compaction (Banigan and Mirny, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: About 50% of metaphase looping events could be sufficient to achieve 100-fold linear chromosome compaction according to theoretical predictions.
source: These events account for about 50% of the total population of metaphase looping events, which, according to theoretical predictions, could be sufficient to achieve 100-fold linear chromosome compaction (Banigan and Mirny, 2018).
evidence: This claim connects experimental observations with theoretical predictions through citation.

claim: The mixed populations of loop extrusion symmetries could play a crucial role for proper chromosome organization in metaphase.
source: Thus, the mixed populations of loop extrusion symmetries we observe could play a crucial role for proper chromosome organization in metaphase.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and theoretical considerations.

claim: Condensin I and condensin II may compact DNA using different symmetries.
source: One possibility is that condensin I and condensin II compact DNA using different symmetries (Kong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citation to a relevant study.

claim: In Xenopus egg extract, the relative abundances of condensin I and condensin II is roughly 5:1.
source: In Xenopus egg extract, the relative abundances of condensin I and condensin II is roughly 5:1 (Ono et al., 2003), which would be consistent with the fraction of nearly symmetric loop extrusion events that we observe in metaphase (~20%).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The 5:1 ratio of condensin I to condensin II would be consistent with the fraction of nearly symmetric loop extrusion events observed in metaphase (~20%).
source: In Xenopus egg extract, the relative abundances of condensin I and condensin II is roughly 5:1 (Ono et al., 2003), which would be consistent with the fraction of nearly symmetric loop extrusion events that we observe in metaphase (~20%).
evidence: This claim connects cited information with experimental observations.

claim: The small population of symmetric loop extrusion in metaphase may arise from residual cohesin activity.
source: As a consequence, we cannot rule out that the small population of symmetric loop extrusion may arise from residual cohesin activity in metaphase.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about an alternative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Extrusion rates and stall forces seem to be conserved during the cell cycle despite differences in loop extrusion symmetries between interphase and metaphase.
source: Despite the differences in loop extrusion symmetries between interphase and metaphase, extrusion rates and stall forces seem to be conserved during the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from both cell cycle phases.

claim: The mean extrusion rates observed are three to four times higher than those observed in previous in vitro studies for cohesin and condensin respectively.
source: The mean extrusion rates we observe, however, are three to four times higher than those observed in previous in vitro studies (Ganji et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019) for cohesin and condensin respectively.
evidence: This claim compares experimental findings with previous in vitro studies through citations.

claim: In extract, several extruding factors may participate in the extrusion of the same DNA loop in a cooperative manner.
source: One possibility for this discrepancy could be that, in extract, several extruding factors participate in the extrusion of the same DNA loop in a cooperative manner.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis to explain the observed higher extrusion rates.

claim: The average stall forces estimated are about five to seven times lower than previous estimates in vitro.
source: However, the average stall forces we estimate are about five to seven times lower than previous estimates in vitro (Ganji et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim compares experimental findings with previous in vitro studies through citations.

claim: In cytoplasmic context of the H3-H4-depleted egg extract, many other DNA-binding factors may compete with the loop extrusion machinery for DNA slack.
source: We speculate that in cytoplasmic context of the H3-H4-depleted egg extract, many other DNA-binding factors—such as linker histone (Xiao et al., 2012)—may compete with the loop extrusion machinery for DNA slack.
evidence: This claim is a speculation to explain the lower stall forces, supported by citation to a relevant study.

claim: Secondary factors could cause the loop extrusion machinery to stop prematurely.
source: The large spread in the distribution of stall forces, with individual examples reaching values that compare to those reported in vitro, may suggest that secondary factors could cause the loop extrusion machinery to stop prematurely, and, consequently, we may underestimate the magnitude of the looping stall forces.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observed distribution of stall forces.

claim: Condensin and cohesin share similar extrusion rates, even though condensin predominantly extrudes non-symmetrically while cohesin extrudes loops symmetrically.
source: We wonder, however, how condensin and cohesin share such similar extrusion rates, even though condensin predominantly extrudes non-symmetrically while cohesin extrudes loops symmetrically.
evidence: This claim is an observation from the experimental data that raises a question.

claim: The similar loop growth velocities would suggest that condensin reels in DNA from one side at twice the rate that cohesin reels in DNA from each of its two sides.
source: The similar loop growth velocities would suggest that condensin reels in DNA from one side at twice the rate that cohesin reels in DNA from each of its two sides.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observed similar extrusion rates.

claim: Cohesin may be a one-sided motor that alternates its extrusion direction.
source: Alternatively, cohesin may be a one-sided motor that alternates its extrusion direction (Banigan et al., 2019)—though we did not observe this kind of switching within the temporal resolution of our measurements.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis supported by citation, with a note about the limitations of the current observations.

claim: Symmetric cohesin loop extrusion could originate from the dimerization of two identical non-symmetric motors.
source: We speculate that symmetric cohesin loop extrusion could originate from the dimerization of two identical non-symmetric motors, though recent in vitro work shows that this idea is controversial (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is a speculation with acknowledgment of controversy based on citations.

claim: On average, symmetric loop extrusion rates in interphase are higher (roughly twice) compared to the non-symmetric events.
source: Interestingly, our results comparing extrusion velocities and corresponding symmetries in interphase show that, on average, symmetric loop extrusion rates are higher (roughly twice) compared to the non-symmetric events (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data and reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The difference in extrusion rates between symmetric and non-symmetric events would be consistent with symmetric and non-symmetric loop extrusion mediated by a dimer and a monomer respectively.
source: This difference in extrusion rates would be consistent with symmetric and non-symmetric loop extrusion mediated by a dimer and a monomer respectively.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the observed difference in extrusion rates.

claim: Lambda-phage DNA was attached to a cover slide using biotin-streptavidin linkers in custom-built microfluidic chambers.
source: To visualize DNA loop formation in Xenopus laevis egg extracts, we attached lambda-phage DNA to a cover slide using biotin-streptavidin linkers (Ganji et al., 2016) in custom-built microfluidic chambers (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method used.

claim: A typical field of view contained 5–20 individual DNA molecules with typically between 2–7 strands having sufficient slack to support loop extrusion.
source: A typical field of view contained 5–20 individual DNA molecules with typically between 2–7 strands having sufficient slack to support loop extrusion.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental conditions.

claim: About 30% of DNA strands with sufficient slack displayed looping events.
source: Of these about 30% displayed looping events (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental observations.
